stem: Four straight lines have the following equations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the gradient of \(L_1\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the gradient of \(L_2\) and the gradient of \(L_3\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which two of the four lines are parallel. Give a reason.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which of the four lines is perpendicular to \(L_1\). Give a reason.

idea: You can read the gradient of a line straight from its equation only when the equation is in the form \(y = mx + c\). Parallel lines have equal gradients, and the gradients of perpendicular lines multiply to give \(-1\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(L_1\) is already in the form \(y = mx + c\), with \(m = 2\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(L_2\): \(4x - 2y = 9\) gives \(2y = 4x - 9\), so \(y = 2x - 4.5\). The gradient is 2.

solution.label: c
steps: \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) both have gradient 2. They have different \(y\)-intercepts, so they are two separate parallel lines.
solution.answer: \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), because they have the same gradient

solution.label: d
steps: A line perpendicular to \(L_1\) must have gradient \(-\dfrac{1}{2} = -0.5\), because \(2 \times (-0.5) = -1\).
\(L_3\) has gradient \(-0.5\). \(L_4\) has gradient \(+0.5\), and \(2 \times 0.5 = 1\), which is not \(-1\), so \(L_4\) is not perpendicular to \(L_1\).

stem: A straight funicular railway runs up a hillside from the lower station \(\mathrm{A}(0,\,150)\) to the upper station \(\mathrm{B}(1200,\,650)\). Here \(x\) is the horizontal distance from A, in metres, and \(y\) is the height above sea level, in metres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the gradient of the track.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down what the gradient tells you about the railway.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the equation of the track in the form \(y = mx + c\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the height of the track above sea level at the point where \(x = 480\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the value of \(x\) at the point where the track is 500 m above sea level.

idea: The gradient of a line is the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\). In a real situation it is a rate: here, metres of height gained for each metre travelled horizontally.

solution.label: b
steps: For each metre travelled horizontally the track rises \(\frac{5}{12}\) of a metre, which is about 0.417 m.
solution.answer: The track rises 5 m for every 12 m travelled horizontally

solution.label: c
steps: The track starts at \((0,\,150)\), so the \(y\)-intercept is 150.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the domain and the range of this model.

idea: A straight-line graph is fixed by where it starts and how steep it is. The domain is the set of \(t\)-values for which the model makes sense, and the range is the set of heights that it gives.

solution.label: a
steps: When \(t = 0\) the line is at \(h = 24\).

solution.label: b
steps: The gradient is negative because the candle is getting shorter.
solution.answer: \(-1.5\): the candle gets 1.5 cm shorter every hour

solution.label: c
steps: Start value 24, gradient \(-1.5\).

solution.label: d
steps: The candle burns from \(t = 0\) until it has gone, at \(t = 16\). During that time its height goes from 24 cm down to 0 cm.

stem: At a market, the price of a basket of strawberries is \(p\) dollars. The number of baskets that customers want to buy is \(D = 500 - 20p\). The number of baskets that growers are willing to sell is \(S = 30p - 150\). Both models are for \(5 \le p \le 25\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(D\) and the value of \(S\) when the price is $10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write down how many more baskets customers want than growers are willing to sell at this price.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the price at which \(D = S\), and the number of baskets sold at this price.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the price at which no customer wants to buy.

idea: Each model is a straight line. One slopes down (a higher price puts customers off) and one slopes up (a higher price attracts sellers). The market settles where the two lines cross.

solution.label: c
steps: Set the two expressions equal: \(500 - 20p = 30p - 150\), so \(650 = 50p\) and \(p = 13\).
You can also plot both lines on your calculator and find the intersection.
At this price \(D = 500 - 20 \times 13 = 240\). Check: \(S = 30 \times 13 - 150 = 240\).

stem: A school has $360 to spend on footballs, which cost $15 each, and basketballs, which cost $24 each. It spends all of the money and buys \(f\) footballs and \(b\) basketballs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down an equation in \(f\) and \(b\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(f\) when \(b = 0\) and the value of \(b\) when \(f = 0\), and state what each value means.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The school buys 8 footballs. Find the number of basketballs that it buys.

parts.label: d
parts.text: When \(b\) is plotted against \(f\), the graph is a straight line. Find its gradient, and state what it means for the school.

idea: A fixed amount of money shared between two kinds of item gives a straight line in the form \(ax + by = c\). The two intercepts are the “all of one kind” choices, and the gradient is the rate at which one item is swapped for the other.

solution.label: a
steps: Money spent on footballs plus money spent on basketballs equals 360.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: \(f = 24\): with no basketballs the school can buy 24 footballs. \(b = 15\): with no footballs it can buy 15 basketballs

solution.label: d
steps: Rearrange: \(24b = 360 - 15f\), so \(b = 15 - 0.625f\). The gradient is \(-0.625 = -\dfrac{5}{8}\).
Each extra football costs the school \(\frac{5}{8}\) of a basketball. In whole numbers: 8 more footballs means 5 fewer basketballs.
solution.answer: \(-0.625\): for every 8 extra footballs the school must buy 5 fewer basketballs

stem: Two machines are tested. The total number of items that each machine has made after \(x\) hours is recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data for machine A can be modelled exactly by a linear function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the data for machine B cannot.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the linear function for machine A, in the form \(y = mx + c\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what the value of \(c\) could mean for machine A.

idea: Data fit a straight line exactly when the gradient between every pair of neighbouring points is the same. Be careful: the \(x\)-values here are not equally spaced, so you must divide by the change in \(x\).

solution.label: a
steps: Gradient between neighbouring points: \(\dfrac{110 - 46}{3 - 1} = 32\), \(\ \dfrac{206 - 110}{6 - 3} = 32\), \(\ \dfrac{334 - 206}{10 - 6} = 32\).
solution.answer: The gradient is 32 each time, so the points lie on one straight line

solution.label: b
solution.answer: The gradients are different, so the points are not on a straight line

solution.label: c
steps: Check with the last point: \(32 \times 10 + 14 = 334\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(c\) is the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\), the number of items at the start of the test.
solution.answer: There were already 14 items made when the test started

stem: The line \(L_1\) has equation \(3x + 4y = 48\). It meets the \(y\)-axis at A and the \(x\)-axis at B. The line \(L_2\) is parallel to \(L_1\) and passes through \(\mathrm{C}(8,\,0)\). It meets the \(y\)-axis at D.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of A and of B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the gradient of \(L_1\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the equation of \(L_2\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the coordinates of D.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the length of [AB] and the length of [CD].

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find the area of the quadrilateral ABCD.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Hence find the perpendicular distance between \(L_1\) and \(L_2\).

idea: ABCD is a trapezium, because [AB] and [DC] are parallel. Its area can be found in two ways: as a large triangle with a small triangle removed, and from the trapezium formula. Putting the two together gives the distance between the parallel sides.

solution.label: c
steps: Parallel lines have the same gradient, so \(L_2\) is \(y = -0.75x + c\).

solution.label: d
steps: The \(y\)-intercept of \(L_2\) is 6.

solution.label: f
steps: Triangle OAB has area \(\frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 12 = 96\). Triangle OCD has area \(\frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24\).
ABCD is what is left when triangle OCD is removed from triangle OAB: \(96 - 24\).

solution.label: g
steps: The area of a trapezium is \(\frac{1}{2}(\text{sum of the parallel sides}) \times (\text{distance between them})\).

stem: A straight line with gradient \(m\), where \(m < 0\), passes through the point \(\mathrm{P}(4,\,3)\). It meets the \(x\)-axis at A and the \(y\)-axis at B. O is the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the \(y\)-coordinate of B is \(3 - 4m\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of \(m\), the \(x\)-coordinate of A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of triangle OAB when \(m = -0.75\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the two values of \(m\) for which the area of triangle OAB is 27.

idea: A line through a known point with gradient \(m\) has equation \(y - 3 = m(x - 4)\). Put \(x = 0\) to find where it crosses the \(y\)-axis and \(y = 0\) to find where it crosses the \(x\)-axis.

solution.label: c
steps: Area \(= \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6\).

solution.label: d
steps: Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(4 - \dfrac{3}{m}\right)(3 - 4m)\). Because \(m\) is negative, both brackets are positive.
Solve \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(4 - \dfrac{3}{m}\right)(3 - 4m) = 27\) on your calculator, for example by graphing the left-hand side for \(m < 0\) and finding where it meets \(y = 27\).
Check: \(m = -1.5\) gives \(\mathrm{OA} = 6\), \(\mathrm{OB} = 9\), area 27. \(\ m = -0.375\) gives \(\mathrm{OA} = 12\), \(\mathrm{OB} = 4.5\), area 27.

idea: \(y\) is a function of \(x\) when each \(x\)-value gives exactly one \(y\)-value. On a graph this means that no vertical line crosses the graph more than once.

solution.label: a
steps: On graph A, a vertical line such as \(x = 2\) crosses the curve twice, at \(y = 2\) and at \(y = -2\). So one \(x\)-value gives two \(y\)-values.
On graphs B and C every vertical line crosses at most once.
solution.answer: Graph A, because some values of \(x\) give two values of \(y\)

solution.label: b
steps: The graph runs from \(x = -3\) to \(x = 3\). Its lowest point is \((0,\,-2)\) and its highest points are the two ends, where \(y = 1\).

stem: The function \(h\) gives the height of a plant, in centimetres, \(w\) weeks after it was planted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the value of \(h(3)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation \(h(w) = 15\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(h^{-1}(8)\), and state what it means for the plant.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the average rate at which the plant grows between week 1 and week 4.

idea: A function takes an input and gives an output: here weeks go in and a height comes out. The inverse function \(h^{-1}\) works backwards: a height goes in and the number of weeks comes out.

solution.label: a
steps: Find 3 in the \(w\) row and read the value below it.

solution.label: b
steps: Find 15 in the \(h(w)\) row and read the value of \(w\) above it.

solution.label: c
steps: \(h^{-1}(8)\) asks which input gives the output 8. From the table, \(h(2) = 8\).
solution.answer: 2: the plant is 8 cm tall 2 weeks after it was planted

solution.label: d
steps: Average rate \(= \dfrac{\text{change in height}}{\text{change in time}} = \dfrac{h(4) - h(1)}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{15 - 5}{3} = 3.33\ldots\)

stem: At an airport desk, \(x\) euros are exchanged for \(f(x)\) dollars, where \(f(x) = 1.08x - 5\), for \(x \ge 20\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of dollars received for 250 euros.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the numbers 1.08 and 5 mean for a customer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find an expression for \(f^{-1}(x)\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of euros that a customer must exchange to receive 400 dollars.

idea: The function turns euros into dollars. Its inverse does the opposite job: it tells you how many euros you need for a given number of dollars. To find it, undo the steps of \(f\) in reverse order.

solution.label: b
steps: 1.08 is the gradient: each extra euro gives 1.08 more dollars. The 5 is taken off whatever the amount, so it is a fixed charge.
solution.answer: 1.08 is the exchange rate, in dollars per euro. 5 is a fixed fee of 5 dollars

solution.label: c
steps: \(f\) multiplies by 1.08 and then subtracts 5. To undo this, add 5 first and then divide by 1.08.
In symbols: \(y = 1.08x - 5\) gives \(x = \dfrac{y + 5}{1.08}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the letter of the graph that matches each description. (i) Ines walks to the park and comes straight back home. (ii) Jon walks to a friend's house, stops there for 10 minutes and then walks on. (iii) Kim runs at first and then slows to a walk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed, in km per hour, of the person in graph A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the speed, in km per hour, of the person in graph D during the first 10 minutes.

idea: On a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed. A steeper line means faster, a horizontal line means not moving, and a line that slopes down means coming back.

solution.label: a
steps: (i) Coming back home means the distance returns to 0: graph C.
(ii) Stopping gives a horizontal section, and then the distance increases again: graph B.
(iii) Fast then slower means steep at first and then less steep: graph D.

solution.label: b
steps: 3 km in 30 minutes. 30 minutes is half an hour, so in a whole hour the person would cover twice as far.

solution.label: c
steps: 2 km in 10 minutes. There are six lots of 10 minutes in an hour: \(2 \times 6\).

stem: A company makes \(n\) chairs in a week. The total cost, in dollars, is \(C(n) = 2450 + 35n + 0.02n^{2}\). The average cost of one chair is \(A(n) = \dfrac{C(n)}{n}\), for \(n \ge 1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the average cost of a chair when 100 chairs are made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of chairs that gives the lowest average cost, and write down this average cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least and the greatest number of chairs for which the average cost is less than $51.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the average cost is very high when only a few chairs are made.

idea: Dividing by \(n\) gives \(A(n) = \dfrac{2450}{n} + 35 + 0.02n\). One part falls as \(n\) grows and another part rises, so the graph comes down, reaches a lowest point and goes up again. Draw it on your calculator.

solution.label: b
steps: Graph \(y = \dfrac{2450}{x} + 35 + 0.02x\) and use the minimum tool: the lowest point is \((350,\,49)\).

solution.label: c
steps: Add the line \(y = 51\) and find the two intersections: \(n = 206.35\ldots\) and \(n = 593.64\ldots\)
The average cost is below $51 between these two values. \(n\) is a whole number, so the first whole number inside is 207 and the last is 593.

solution.label: d
steps: The $2450 has to be paid however many chairs are made. With few chairs, each one carries a large share of it: for example \(2450 \div 5 = 490\) dollars per chair.
solution.answer: The fixed cost of $2450 is shared between only a few chairs

stem: Let \(f(x) = 1.5^{x} - 2\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the domain and the range of \(f^{-1}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the \(x\)-coordinates of the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the graph of \(f^{-1}\).

idea: You do not need a formula for \(f^{-1}\). Finding \(f^{-1}(k)\) means solving \(f(x) = k\). The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the graph of \(f\) reflected in the line \(y = x\), so the domain and range swap over.

solution.label: a
steps: As \(x\) becomes very negative, \(1.5^{x}\) gets close to 0, so \(f(x)\) gets close to \(-2\).

solution.label: c
steps: On the calculator (graph or solver), \(x = 3\). Check: \(1.5^{3} = 3.375\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(f\) has domain all real numbers and range \(y > -2\), because \(1.5^{x}\) is always positive. For the inverse these swap.

solution.label: e
steps: \(f\) is an increasing function, so its graph can only meet its reflection on the mirror line \(y = x\). Solve \(f(x) = x\).
Graph \(y = 1.5^{x} - 2\) and \(y = x\) and find the intersections: \(x = -1.442\ldots\) and \(x = 4.686\ldots\)

stem: The diagram shows the graph of a quadratic function \(f\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the zeros of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the minimum value of \(f\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the values of \(x\) for which \(f(x) < 0\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: The graph passes through \((0,\,5)\). Write down the coordinates of the other point on the graph that has \(y\)-coordinate 5.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Write down the range of \(f\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

idea: A parabola is symmetrical about the vertical line through its vertex. Every point on one side has a partner at the same height on the other side, the same distance from that line.

solution.label: a
steps: The zeros are where the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis.

solution.label: b
steps: The axis of symmetry is halfway between the zeros, \(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2} = 3\), and passes through the vertex.

solution.label: c
steps: The lowest point of the graph is the vertex \((3,\,-4)\). The minimum value is its \(y\)-coordinate.

solution.label: d
steps: \(f(x) < 0\) where the graph is below the \(x\)-axis, which is between the two zeros.

solution.label: e
steps: \((0,\,5)\) is 3 units to the left of the axis of symmetry, so its partner is 3 units to the right, at \(x = 6\).

solution.label: f
steps: The graph goes no lower than \(-4\) and rises without limit on both sides.

stem: The stopping distance of a car, \(d\) metres, when it is travelling at \(v\) km per hour is modelled by \(d(v) = 0.006v^{2} + 0.2v\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the stopping distance at 50 km per hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the stopping distance at 100 km per hour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lena says that doubling the speed doubles the stopping distance. State whether the model agrees with her, and give a reason.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the speed at which the stopping distance is 40 m.

idea: The \(v^{2}\) term makes this a quadratic model. Quadratic models grow faster and faster, so doubling the input does more than double the output.

solution.label: c
steps: From 50 to 100 km per hour the speed doubles, but the stopping distance goes from 25 m to 80 m, and \(80 \div 25 = 3.2\).
solution.answer: No. The stopping distance is 3.2 times as long, not twice as long

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(0.006v^{2} + 0.2v = 40\) on your calculator. The solutions are \(v = 66.66\ldots\) and \(v = -100\). A speed cannot be negative.

stem: In a league, each team plays every other team once. When there are \(n\) teams, the total number of matches is \(M(n) = 0.5n^{2} - 0.5n\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of matches in a league of 6 teams.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of matches in a league of 20 teams.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A league has 66 matches. Find the number of teams.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the total number of matches in a league of this kind cannot be 50.

idea: Going forwards, from teams to matches, is a substitution. Going backwards, from matches to teams, means solving a quadratic equation, and only a whole-number answer makes sense.

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(0.5n^{2} - 0.5n = 66\) on your calculator: \(n = 12\) or \(n = -11\). The number of teams is positive.

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(0.5n^{2} - 0.5n = 50\): the positive solution is \(n = 10.51\ldots\), which is not a whole number.
You can also see it from a table: 10 teams give 45 matches and 11 teams give 55, so 50 is skipped.
solution.answer: The equation \(M(n) = 50\) has no whole-number solution: 10 teams give 45 matches and 11 teams give 55

stem: The fuel efficiency of a car, \(E\) km per litre, depends on its speed, \(v\) km per hour. It is modelled by \(E = av^{2} + bv + c\). In tests the car managed 14.4 km per litre at 40 km per hour, 16.8 km per litre at 60 km per hour and 15.6 km per litre at 100 km per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down three equations in \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the speed at which the car is most efficient, and its fuel efficiency at this speed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the model to estimate the fuel efficiency at 130 km per hour.

idea: A quadratic model has three unknown numbers, so three measurements are needed to fix it. Each measurement gives one equation, and the simultaneous equation solver finds \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

solution.label: a
steps: Substitute each speed and efficiency into \(E = av^{2} + bv + c\). For example, \(40^{2} = 1600\).

solution.label: b
steps: Enter the three equations in the simultaneous equation solver.

solution.label: c
steps: Graph \(E = -0.0025v^{2} + 0.37v + 3.6\) and use the maximum tool. The vertex is at \(v = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{0.37}{0.005} = 74\).
solution.answer: 74 km per hour; 17.3 km per litre

solution.label: d
steps: 130 km per hour is outside the range of the tests (40 to 100), so this is an extrapolation and should be treated with care.

stem: The number of people at a one-day festival, \(t\) hours after the gates open, is modelled by \(N(t) = -45t^{2} + 540t\), for \(0 \le t \le 12\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of people at the festival 2 hours after the gates open.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest number of people at the festival, and the time at which this happens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the two times at which there are 1400 people at the festival, and hence find for how long there are more than 1400 people.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the model stops at \(t = 12\).

idea: The graph is a parabola that opens downwards: the crowd builds up, reaches a peak and then falls away. Questions about “more than” a number are answered by finding where the graph crosses that height.

solution.label: b
steps: Use the maximum tool on the graph, or the axis of symmetry \(t = -\dfrac{540}{2 \times (-45)} = 6\).
solution.answer: 1620 people, 6 hours after the gates open

solution.label: c
steps: The graph is above 1400 between these times: \(8.211\ldots - 3.788\ldots = 4.422\ldots\) hours.

solution.label: d
steps: \(N(12) = -45 \times 144 + 540 \times 12 = 0\), so by then everyone has left. After \(t = 12\) the formula gives negative numbers of people, which is impossible.
solution.answer: \(N(12) = 0\), and for larger \(t\) the model gives a negative number of people

stem: An orchard has 40 apple trees, and each tree produces 500 apples in a season. If more trees are planted the trees are crowded, and for each extra tree every tree produces 10 fewer apples. When \(x\) extra trees are planted, the total number of apples is \(Y(x) = (40 + x)(500 - 10x)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the total number of apples produced now.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of extra trees that gives the greatest total number of apples, and find this total.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of extra trees, other than zero, for which the total is the same as it is now.

idea: Total = (number of trees) × (apples on each tree). Planting more trees pushes the first number up and the second number down, and the product of the two is a quadratic with a maximum.

solution.label: b
steps: Collect the \(x\) terms: \(-400x + 500x = 100x\).

solution.label: c
steps: The maximum is on the axis of symmetry, \(x = -\dfrac{100}{2 \times (-10)} = 5\).

solution.label: d
steps: This fits the symmetry of the parabola: 0 and 10 are the same distance from the axis \(x = 5\). Check: \(50 \times 400 = 20\,000\).

stem: A rectangular swimming pool is 12 m long and 8 m wide. A path of width \(x\) metres is to be built all the way round the pool.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area of the path is \(A(x) = 4x^{2} + 40x\) square metres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the path when its width is 1.5 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the width of a path that has an area of exactly 120 m\(^2\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Paving for the path costs $45 per square metre. A fence is to be put along the outside edge of the path, at a cost of $12 per metre. Show that the total cost, in dollars, is \(180x^{2} + 1896x + 480\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the width of the path for which the total cost is exactly $6000.

idea: The pool and the path together make a larger rectangle. Each of its sides is longer than the pool's by \(2x\), because the path adds a width \(x\) at both ends.

solution.label: a
steps: The outer rectangle measures \((12 + 2x)\) by \((8 + 2x)\). The path is the outer rectangle with the pool removed.
\[\begin{aligned}&(12 + 2x)(8 + 2x) - 12 \times 8 \\[4pt] &= 96 + 24x + 16x + 4x^{2} - 96\end{aligned}\]

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(4x^{2} + 40x = 120\) on your calculator: \(x = 2.416\ldots\) or \(x = -12.4\ldots\) A width is positive.

solution.label: d
steps: The outside edge is the perimeter of the outer rectangle: \(2(12 + 2x) + 2(8 + 2x) = 40 + 8x\) metres. Fence: \(12(40 + 8x) = 480 + 96x\).

solution.label: e
steps: Solve \(180x^{2} + 1896x + 480 = 6000\) on your calculator: the positive solution is \(x = 2.375\ldots\)

stem: The main cable of a suspension bridge hangs between two towers that are 100 m apart. The height of the cable above the road, in metres, is modelled by \(h(x) = 0.008x^{2} - 0.8x + 25\), for \(0 \le x \le 100\), where \(x\) metres is the horizontal distance from the left-hand tower.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the height above the road at which the cable is attached to the left-hand tower.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the lowest point of the cable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the values of \(x\) at which the cable is 10 m above the road.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A second cable is attached to the towers at the same two points. Its height above the road is \(g(x) = a(x - 50)^{2} + 10\). Find the value of \(a\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the vertical distance between the two cables at \(x = 20\).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Write down the greatest vertical distance between the two cables.

idea: Both cables are parabolas with the same axis of symmetry, \(x = 50\), halfway between the towers. They share their end points, so they differ most in the middle.

solution.label: a
steps: At the left-hand tower \(x = 0\), and \(h(0) = 25\).

solution.label: b
steps: Use the minimum tool, or the axis of symmetry \(x = -\dfrac{-0.8}{2 \times 0.008} = 50\).

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(0.008x^{2} - 0.8x + 25 = 10\) on your calculator.
The two answers are the same distance, 25 m, either side of the middle of the bridge.

solution.label: d
steps: The second cable also passes through \((0,\,25)\): \(a(0 - 50)^{2} + 10 = 25\), so \(2500a = 15\).

solution.label: f
steps: The cables meet at the towers and are furthest apart in the middle, where their heights are 10 m and 5 m.

stem: A workshop makes and sells \(x\) wooden toys each week. The total cost of making them, in dollars, is \(C(x) = 0.5x^{2} + 20x + 800\). Each toy is sold for $90.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the cost in a week in which no toys are made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the weekly profit is \(P(x) = -0.5x^{2} + 70x - 800\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the profit in a week in which 20 toys are made and sold.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the least and the greatest whole number of toys for which the workshop makes a profit.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the number of toys that gives the greatest profit, and find this profit.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find the least and the greatest whole number of toys for which the profit is at least $1000.

parts.label: g
parts.text: The rent of the workshop goes up, so the fixed cost of $800 increases. Find the greatest fixed cost for which the workshop can still make a profit of $1000 in a week.

idea: Profit is the money that comes in minus the money that goes out: \(P(x) = R(x) - C(x)\), where the revenue is \(R(x) = 90x\). The profit graph is a parabola that opens downwards, and each part of the question is about where it sits relative to a horizontal line.

solution.label: a
steps: \(C(0) = 800\). This is the fixed cost: rent, for example, has to be paid even if nothing is made.

solution.label: b
steps: Revenue from \(x\) toys is \(90x\).
\[\begin{aligned}P(x) &= 90x - \left(0.5x^{2} + 20x + 800\right) \\[4pt] &= 90x - 0.5x^{2} - 20x - 800\end{aligned}\]

solution.label: d
steps: Find the zeros of \(P\): \(x = 12.55\ldots\) and \(x = 127.4\ldots\) The profit is positive between them.
\(x\) is a whole number, so the first value inside is 13 and the last is 127. Check: \(P(12) = -32\) and \(P(13) = 25.5\); \(\ P(127) = 25.5\) and \(P(128) = -32\).

solution.label: e
steps: Use the maximum tool, or the axis of symmetry \(x = -\dfrac{70}{2 \times (-0.5)} = 70\).

solution.label: f
steps: Solve \(P(x) = 1000\): \(x = 33.94\ldots\) and \(x = 106.05\ldots\) The profit is at least 1000 between them.

solution.label: g
steps: A larger fixed cost moves the whole profit graph straight down. The best week is still 70 toys, where the profit before the fixed cost is taken off is \(1650 + 800 = 2450\) dollars.
For a profit of 1000 to be possible, the fixed cost can be at most \(2450 - 1000\).

stem: Light gets weaker as it travels down through sea water. Each metre of water absorbs 16 % of the light that enters it. At the surface the light is at 100 % of its full strength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the percentage of the light that is left after 1 metre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that about 59.3 % of the light is left at a depth of 3 metres.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down a model for \(L(d)\), the percentage of the light that is left at a depth of \(d\) metres.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the depth at which only 10 % of the light is left.

idea: Losing 16 % is the same as keeping 84 %, which means multiplying by 0.84. Doing this once for every metre gives an exponential model.

solution.label: b
steps: Each metre multiplies the light by 0.84, so three metres multiply it by \(0.84^{3}\).

solution.label: c
steps: Start at 100 and multiply by 0.84 once for each metre.

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(100 \times 0.84^{d} = 10\) on your calculator, with the solver or by finding where the graph meets \(y = 10\): \(d = 13.20\ldots\)

stem: The diagram shows the graphs of four functions.
The four functions are \(\ y = 2 \times 1.5^{x}\), \(\ \ y = 2 \times 0.5^{x}\), \(\ \ y = 2 \times 1.5^{x} + 3\ \) and \(\ y = 4 - 2 \times 0.5^{x}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the letter of the graph of (i) \(y = 2 \times 1.5^{x}\); (ii) \(y = 2 \times 0.5^{x}\); (iii) \(y = 4 - 2 \times 0.5^{x}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of \(y = 2 \times 1.5^{x} + 3\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the \(y\)-intercept of the graph of \(y = 4 - 2 \times 0.5^{x}\).

idea: Three things identify an exponential graph: where it crosses the \(y\)-axis (put \(x = 0\)), whether it rises or falls, and the height that it levels off towards (its asymptote).

solution.label: a
steps: (i) \(2 \times 1.5^{x}\) passes through \((0,\,2)\), rises faster and faster, and gets close to the \(x\)-axis on the left: graph D.
(ii) \(2 \times 0.5^{x}\) passes through \((0,\,2)\) and falls, because the base 0.5 is less than 1: graph A.
(iii) \(4 - 2 \times 0.5^{x}\) passes through \((0,\,2)\) and rises, but the part being taken away shrinks, so it levels off below 4: graph B.
That leaves graph C for \(2 \times 1.5^{x} + 3\), which passes through \((0,\,5)\).

solution.label: b
steps: On the left, \(2 \times 1.5^{x}\) gets close to 0, so \(y\) gets close to 3.

stem: Duckweed is spreading over the surface of a pond. The area that it covers is measured at the same time each day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area is multiplied by the same number each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down a model for \(A(t)\), the area covered on day \(t\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area that the model gives for day 10.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The pond has an area of 60 m\(^2\). Find the first day on which the model gives an area greater than this.

idea: If each value is the one before multiplied by the same number, the data follow an exponential model \(A(t) = k \times a^{t}\), where \(k\) is the starting value and \(a\) is the multiplier.

solution.label: a
steps: Divide each area by the one before: \(5 \div 4 = 1.25\), \(\ 6.25 \div 5 = 1.25\), \(\ 7.8125 \div 6.25 = 1.25\).

solution.label: b
steps: Starting value 4, multiplier 1.25.

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(4 \times 1.25^{t} = 60\): \(t = 12.13\ldots\) The measurements are made once a day, so look at whole days.
Day 12 gives \(58.2\ldots\) m\(^2\), which is not enough. Day 13 gives \(72.7\ldots\) m\(^2\).

stem: The brightness of a glow stick, \(B\) lux, \(t\) hours after it is switched on is modelled by \(B(t) = 60\mathrm{e}^{-0.35t}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the brightness of the glow stick when it is switched on.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the brightness after 2 hours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the brightness falls by about 29.5 % each hour.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the time at which the brightness is one quarter of its starting value.

idea: \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.35t}\) is the same as \(\left(\mathrm{e}^{-0.35}\right)^{t}\). So this is an ordinary exponential model in disguise, and its hourly multiplier is the number \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.35}\).

solution.label: c
steps: Each hour the brightness is multiplied by \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.35} = 0.7046\ldots\)
So 70.46… % is kept each hour, and \(100 - 70.46\ldots = 29.53\ldots\) % is lost.
solution.answer: \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.35} = 0.7046\ldots\), so about 29.5 % is lost each hour

solution.label: d
steps: A quarter of 60 is 15. Solve \(60\mathrm{e}^{-0.35t} = 15\) on your calculator: \(t = 3.960\ldots\)

stem: The number of homes in a town that have solar panels is modelled by \(N(t) = k \times a^{t}\), where \(t\) is the number of years after the start of 2015. The town had 720 homes with solar panels at \(t = 2\) and 2430 at \(t = 5\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(a = 1.5\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(k\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of homes with solar panels that the model gives for \(t = 8\), to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The town has 9000 homes. Find the value of \(t\) at which the model reaches 9000, and explain why the model cannot be correct after this.

idea: From \(t = 2\) to \(t = 5\) is three years, so the number is multiplied by \(a\) three times. Dividing the later value by the earlier one removes \(k\) and leaves \(a^{3}\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(ka^{2} = 720\) and \(ka^{5} = 2430\). Divide the second by the first:
Take the cube root: \(a = \sqrt[3]{3.375}\).

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(320 \times 1.5^{t} = 9000\) on your calculator: \(t = 8.229\ldots\)
After that the model gives more homes with solar panels than there are homes in the town.
solution.answer: \(t = 8.23\). Beyond this the model gives more than the 9000 homes that exist

stem: A new café can serve at most 180 customers a day. On its first day it has 30 customers, which is 150 below the maximum. Each week, the gap between the number of customers and the maximum becomes 15 % smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the size of the gap after 1 week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the café has about 88 customers a day after 3 weeks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down a model for \(N(t)\), the number of customers a day after \(t\) weeks.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of complete weeks needed for the gap to be less than 15 customers.

idea: The thing that shrinks exponentially here is the gap, not the number of customers. Model the gap first, then take it away from 180. This gives a curve that climbs towards 180 and levels off.

solution.label: a
steps: 15 % smaller means multiplied by 0.85: \(150 \times 0.85\).

solution.label: b
steps: Gap after 3 weeks: \(150 \times 0.85^{3} = 92.11\ldots\)
Customers: \(180 - 92.11\ldots = 87.88\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The gap after \(t\) weeks is \(150 \times 0.85^{t}\). The number of customers is 180 minus the gap.

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(150 \times 0.85^{t} = 15\) on your calculator: \(t = 14.16\ldots\) Round up to a complete week.
Check: after 14 weeks the gap is \(15.41\ldots\), and after 15 weeks it is \(13.10\ldots\)

stem: Town A has a population of 42 000, which is falling by 1.5 % each year. Town B has a population of 28 000, which is rising by 2.5 % each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a model for the population of each town after \(t\) years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the population of each town after 10 years. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of complete years after which town B first has the larger population.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the percentage change in the total population of the two towns over the first 10 years.

idea: A fall of 1.5 % a year is a multiplier of 0.985, and a rise of 2.5 % a year is a multiplier of 1.025. The two populations are two exponential curves, one going down and one going up, and they cross.

solution.label: a
steps: Start value × multiplier to the power \(t\), for each town.

solution.label: c
steps: After 10 years town A is still slightly larger. Find where the graphs cross: \(42\,000 \times 0.985^{t} = 28\,000 \times 1.025^{t}\) gives \(t = 10.18\ldots\)
Round up. Check: after 11 years A has \(35\,567.0\ldots\) and B has \(36\,738.4\ldots\)

stem: A glass of lemonade is poured, and the height of the foam on top, \(h\) mm, is measured every minute.
Time, \(t\) minutes: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: By finding the change in height during each minute, show that a linear model does not fit the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By dividing each height by the one before it, show that an exponential model is suitable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down an exponential model for \(h\) in terms of \(t\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: At \(t = 6\) the measured height of the foam is 15.1 mm. Find the percentage error in the value that the model gives.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Use the model to find the time at which the height of the foam is 5 mm.

parts.label: f
parts.text: A linear model through the first two measurements is \(h = 80 - 20t\). Explain why this model cannot be right for \(t = 5\).

idea: Two quick tests tell you which kind of model fits a table of equally spaced data. If the differences are constant, use a linear model. If the ratios are constant, use an exponential model.

solution.label: a
steps: A linear model needs the same change every minute.
solution.answer: The changes are \(-20,\ -15,\ -11.2,\ -8.5\), which are not constant

solution.label: b
steps: Measurements are never perfect, so ratios this close to each other count as constant.
solution.answer: Each height is about 0.75 times the one before

solution.label: c
steps: Starting value 80, multiplier 0.75.

solution.label: d
steps: Model: \(80 \times 0.75^{6} = 14.238\ldots\) The measured value, 15.1, is the exact value here, and the model's value is the approximation.
\[\varepsilon = \left|\frac{14.238\ldots - 15.1}{15.1}\right| \times 100 = 5.706\ldots\]
Keep the unrounded 14.238… on your calculator for this step.

solution.label: e
steps: Solve \(80 \times 0.75^{t} = 5\) on your calculator: \(t = 9.637\ldots\)

solution.label: f
steps: \(80 - 20 \times 5 = -20\). A height cannot be negative. (The linear model reaches zero at \(t = 4\), when there is really still 25.3 mm of foam.)
solution.answer: It gives a height of \(-20\) mm, which is impossible

stem: In 1971 a computer chip contained 2300 transistors. Since then the number of transistors on the most powerful chip has roughly doubled every two years. This is modelled by \(N(t) = 2300 \times 2^{\frac{t}{2}}\), where \(t\) is the number of years after 1971.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value that the model gives for 1981.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the model increases by about 41.4 % each year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the smallest whole number \(t\) for which the model gives more than one billion (\(10^{9}\)) transistors, and write down the year that this represents.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A chip made in 2020 contained \(1.6 \times 10^{10}\) transistors. Find the percentage error in the value that the model gives for 2020.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A better model for recent years is \(N(t) = 2300 \times 2^{\frac{t}{d}}\), in which the number doubles every \(d\) years. Find the value of \(d\) for which this model gives the correct number of transistors for 2020.

idea: Doubling every two years means the exponent goes up by 1 every two years, which is why it is \(\frac{t}{2}\). In one year the exponent goes up by a half, so the yearly multiplier is \(2^{0.5}\).

solution.label: b
steps: When \(t\) goes up by 1, the exponent \(\frac{t}{2}\) goes up by 0.5, so \(N\) is multiplied by \(2^{0.5} = 1.4142\ldots\)
A multiplier of 1.4142… is an increase of 41.42… %.
solution.answer: \(2^{0.5} = 1.4142\ldots\), an increase of about 41.4 % a year

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(2300 \times 2^{\frac{t}{2}} = 10^{9}\) on your calculator: \(t = 37.45\ldots\) The first whole number above this is 38.
Check: \(t = 37\) gives about \(8.5 \times 10^{8}\), which is not enough, and \(t = 38\) gives about \(1.2 \times 10^{9}\).

solution.label: d
steps: \[\varepsilon = \left|\frac{5.457\ldots \times 10^{10} - 1.6 \times 10^{10}}{1.6 \times 10^{10}}\right| \times 100 = 241.0\ldots\]
The model gives more than three times the real number. The doubling has slowed down, so the model no longer fits.

solution.label: e
steps: The new model must give \(1.6 \times 10^{10}\) when \(t = 49\): solve \(2300 \times 2^{\frac{49}{d}} = 1.6 \times 10^{10}\) for \(d\) with your calculator's solver.
\(d = 2.155\ldots\) So over the whole period the number has doubled about every 2.16 years, a little more slowly than every 2 years.
A small change in the doubling time makes a very large difference after 49 years, which is why the error in part (d) is so big.

stem: The mass, \(m\) grams, of a solid steel ball varies directly with the cube of its radius, \(r\) cm. A ball of radius 2 cm has a mass of 264 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find an equation for \(m\) in terms of \(r\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the mass of a ball of radius 3 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the radius of a ball of mass 4125 g.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The radius of a ball is doubled. Write down the number that its mass is multiplied by.

idea: “Varies directly with the cube” means \(m = kr^{3}\) for some constant \(k\). One pair of values is enough to find \(k\).

solution.label: d
steps: Doubling \(r\) multiplies \(r^{3}\) by \(2^{3}\).

stem: A swimming pool is filled using identical pumps. The time taken, \(t\) hours, depends on the number of pumps, \(n\).
Number of pumps, \(n\): 2, 3, 4, 6
Time, \(t\) hours: 18, 12, 9, 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(t\) varies inversely with \(n\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down an equation for \(t\) in terms of \(n\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the time taken to fill the pool with 8 pumps.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the least number of pumps needed to fill the pool in less than 2.5 hours.

idea: Two quantities vary inversely when their product is always the same: doubling one halves the other. The model is \(t = \dfrac{k}{n}\), where \(k\) is that constant product.

solution.label: a
steps: Multiply each pair: \(2 \times 18 = 36\), \(\ 3 \times 12 = 36\), \(\ 4 \times 9 = 36\), \(\ 6 \times 6 = 36\).
solution.answer: \(n \times t = 36\) every time, so \(t\) varies inversely with \(n\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(nt = 36\), rearranged.

solution.label: d
steps: Solve \(\dfrac{36}{n} < 2.5\): \(n > 36 \div 2.5 = 14.4\). The number of pumps is a whole number, so round up.
Check: 14 pumps take \(2.57\ldots\) hours and 15 pumps take 2.4 hours.

stem: At a restaurant, the price of a round pizza, \(C\) dollars, varies directly with the square of its diameter, \(d\) cm. A pizza with a diameter of 20 cm costs $6.40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find an equation for \(C\) in terms of \(d\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the price of a pizza with a diameter of 30 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the diameter of a pizza that costs $25.60.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Sam says that a pizza with twice the diameter should cost twice as much. Explain why the model does not agree with Sam, and write down the number that the price is multiplied by.

idea: “Varies directly with the square” means \(C = kd^{2}\). This makes sense for a pizza, because the amount of pizza depends on its area, and area depends on the square of the diameter.

solution.label: d
steps: Doubling \(d\) multiplies \(d^{2}\) by \(2^{2} = 4\), so the price is multiplied by 4. Parts (a) and (c) show this: 20 cm costs $6.40 and 40 cm costs $25.60.
This is fair, because a pizza with twice the diameter has four times the area.
solution.answer: The price depends on \(d^{2}\), so it is multiplied by 4, not by 2

stem: Some air is trapped in a syringe. Its pressure, \(P\) kPa, varies inversely with its volume, \(V\) cm\(^3\). The pressure is 150 kPa when the volume is 24 cm\(^3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find an equation for \(P\) in terms of \(V\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the pressure when the volume is 40 cm\(^3\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume at which the pressure is 400 kPa.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The volume of the air is reduced by 20 %. Find the percentage increase in the pressure.

idea: “Varies inversely” means \(P = \dfrac{k}{V}\). When the volume is multiplied by a number, the pressure is divided by the same number.

solution.label: d
steps: Reducing the volume by 20 % multiplies it by 0.8. The pressure is then divided by 0.8, and \(1 \div 0.8 = 1.25\).
A multiplier of 1.25 is an increase of 25 %. (Check with numbers: at 24 cm\(^3\) the pressure is 150 kPa, and at \(0.8 \times 24 = 19.2\) cm\(^3\) it is \(3600 \div 19.2 = 187.5\) kPa.)

stem: After a meal, the level of glucose in Tara's blood, \(G\) millimoles per litre, is modelled by \(G(t) = 0.45t^{3} - 2.9t^{2} + 4.4t + 5\), for \(0 \le t \le 4\), where \(t\) is the time in hours after the meal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the glucose level at the time of the meal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the highest glucose level, and the time at which it occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the time at which the glucose level first returns to its value at the time of the meal.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the lowest glucose level during the 4 hours.

parts.label: e
parts.text: By finding \(G(8)\), explain why the model should not be used for \(t = 8\).

idea: A cubic model can rise, fall and rise again, which suits a quantity that overshoots and then settles. Draw the graph on your calculator for \(0 \le t \le 4\) and use the maximum, minimum and intersection tools.

solution.label: b
steps: Use the maximum tool: the highest point is at \(t = 0.983\ldots\), where \(G = 6.950\ldots\)
solution.answer: 6.95 millimoles per litre, 0.984 hours (about 59 minutes) after the meal

solution.label: c
steps: Add the line \(y = 5\) and find where the graph meets it after \(t = 0\): \(t = 2.444\ldots\) (and again at \(t = 4\)).

solution.label: d
steps: Use the minimum tool: the lowest point is at \(t = 3.312\ldots\), where \(G = 4.110\ldots\) This is lower than the value 5 at both ends.

solution.label: e
steps: \(G(8) = 0.45 \times 512 - 2.9 \times 64 + 4.4 \times 8 + 5 = 85\). A glucose level of 85 is impossibly high: the model only describes the 4 hours after the meal.
solution.answer: \(G(8) = 85\), far above any possible level, so the model fails outside \(0 \le t \le 4\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(V(12)\), and show that it is equal to the volume of a hemisphere of radius 12 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the volume of water when the depth is 6 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage of the bowl that is filled when the depth is 6 cm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the depth of the water when the bowl contains 2000 cm\(^3\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the depth of the water when the bowl is half full.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Explain, using the shape of the bowl, why the answer to part (e) is more than 6 cm.

idea: Multiplied out, \(V(h) = 12\pi h^{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}h^{3}\), so this is a cubic model. Going from a depth to a volume is a substitution. Going from a volume to a depth means solving a cubic equation with your calculator.

solution.label: a
steps: \(V(12) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \times 144 \times 24 = 1152\pi = 3619.1\ldots\)
A hemisphere is half a sphere: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi \times 12^{3} = 1152\pi\). The two agree.

solution.label: b
steps: \(V(6) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \times 36 \times 30 = 360\pi = 1130.9\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: Graph \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{3}x^{2}(36 - x)\) for \(0 \le x \le 12\) and find where it meets \(y = 2000\): \(h = 8.304\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Half of the full volume is \(576\pi = 1809.5\ldots\) cm\(^3\). Find where the graph meets this height: \(h = 7.832\ldots\)

solution.label: f
steps: The bowl is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top. The bottom 6 cm of depth holds much less water than the top 6 cm (only 31.25 % of the total, from part (c)), so the water has to rise above the halfway depth to reach half the volume.
solution.answer: The bowl is narrower near the bottom, so the lower half of the depth holds less than half of the water

stem: The force of air resistance on a cyclist, \(F\) newtons, is modelled by \(F = av^{n}\), where \(v\) is the speed in metres per second, \(a\) is a constant and \(n\) is a positive integer. The force is 6 N at a speed of 5 m s\(^{-1}\) and 24 N at a speed of 10 m s\(^{-1}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(n = 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The power, \(P\) watts, that the cyclist needs to overcome air resistance is \(P = F \times v\). Show that \(P = 0.24v^{3}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the power needed at a speed of 12 m s\(^{-1}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: The cyclist can produce 300 W. Find her greatest possible speed.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find the percentage increase in power that is needed to increase any speed by 20 %.

parts.label: g
parts.text: The cyclist now rides into a wind of 3 m s\(^{-1}\). The force of air resistance is now \(F = 0.24(v + 3)^{2}\). The power needed is still \(P = F \times v\). Find her greatest possible speed now, if she can produce 300 W.

idea: In a power model \(y = ax^{n}\), multiplying \(x\) by a number multiplies \(y\) by that number to the power \(n\). Comparing two measurements shows what \(n\) must be.

solution.label: a
steps: From 5 to 10 m s\(^{-1}\) the speed is multiplied by 2, and the force is multiplied by \(24 \div 6 = 4\).
In \(F = av^{n}\), doubling \(v\) multiplies \(F\) by \(2^{n}\). So \(2^{n} = 4\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(P = F \times v = 0.24v^{2} \times v\)

solution.label: f
steps: Increasing \(v\) by 20 % multiplies it by 1.2. Because \(P\) depends on \(v^{3}\), the power is multiplied by \(1.2^{3} = 1.728\).
A multiplier of 1.728 is an increase of 72.8 %. This is why going a little faster on a bicycle feels so much harder.

solution.label: g
steps: The power is now \(P = 0.24(v + 3)^{2} \times v\). This can no longer be rearranged neatly, so use a graph or the solver for \[0.24v(v + 3)^{2} = 300\]
\(v = 8.870\ldots\) The wind costs her almost 2 m s\(^{-1}\) compared with part (e).

stem: The diagram shows the graph of \(y = a\sin(bx^\circ) + d\), for \(0 \le x \le 16\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the maximum value and the minimum value of \(y\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the value of \(a\), the amplitude.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the equation of the principal axis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the period.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the value of \(b\).

idea: Every sine graph has a middle line (the principal axis), a height above and below that line (the amplitude) and a length after which it repeats (the period). For \(y = a\sin(bx^\circ) + d\), the period is \(\dfrac{360}{b}\).

solution.label: a
steps: The highest points are at \(y = 5\) and the lowest are at \(y = -1\).

solution.label: b
steps: The amplitude is half the distance between the maximum and the minimum: \(\dfrac{5 - (-1)}{2}\).

solution.label: c
steps: The principal axis is halfway between the maximum and the minimum: \(\dfrac{5 + (-1)}{2} = 2\). This is the value of \(d\).

solution.label: d
steps: One complete wave runs from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 8\). (Maximum to next maximum, from \(x = 2\) to \(x = 10\), gives the same.)

stem: While Mia is resting, the volume of air in her lungs, \(V\) litres, \(t\) seconds after she starts to breathe in is modelled by \(V(t) = 0.5\sin(72t^\circ) + 2.4\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the greatest and the least volume of air in Mia's lungs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time that Mia takes for one complete breath, in and out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of breaths that Mia takes in one minute.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the volume of air in Mia's lungs when \(t = 2\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write down the volume of air that Mia breathes in during one breath.

idea: In \(V(t) = a\sin(bt^\circ) + d\), the value of \(d\) is the middle volume, \(a\) is how far the volume moves above and below the middle, and \(\dfrac{360}{b}\) is the time for one complete cycle.

solution.label: a
steps: The sine part moves between \(-0.5\) and \(+0.5\), so the volume moves between \(2.4 - 0.5\) and \(2.4 + 0.5\).

solution.label: b
steps: One breath is one period: \(\dfrac{360}{72}\).

solution.label: d
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(V(2) = 0.5\sin(144^\circ) + 2.4 = 2.693\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: During one breath in, the volume rises from its least value to its greatest value: \(2.9 - 1.9\). This is twice the amplitude.

stem: A horse on a carousel moves up and down. Its height above the platform varies between 0.9 m and 1.5 m, and it takes 4 seconds to go up, down and back to where it started. At \(t = 0\) the horse is at its middle height and moving upwards. Its height, \(h\) metres, after \(t\) seconds is modelled by \(h(t) = a\sin(bt^\circ) + d\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(d\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(b\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the height of the horse when \(t = 5.5\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the first two times at which the height of the horse is 1.35 m.

idea: Build the model from three facts: the middle height gives \(d\), the distance from the middle to the top gives \(a\), and the time for one cycle gives \(b\) through \(\text{period} = \dfrac{360}{b}\).

solution.label: a
steps: The amplitude is half of the distance between the highest and lowest heights: \(\dfrac{1.5 - 0.9}{2}\).

solution.label: b
steps: The middle height is halfway between 0.9 and 1.5: \(\dfrac{1.5 + 0.9}{2}\).

solution.label: c
steps: The period is 4 seconds, so \(\dfrac{360}{b} = 4\).

solution.label: d
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(h(5.5) = 0.3\sin(495^\circ) + 1.2 = 1.412\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Graph \(y = 0.3\sin(90x^\circ) + 1.2\) and \(y = 1.35\), and find the first two intersections: \(t = 0.333\ldots\) and \(t = 1.666\ldots\)
The horse passes 1.35 m once on the way up and once on the way down.

stem: The average monthly temperature in a city, \(T\) °C, is modelled by \(T(m) = 14 - 9\cos(30m^\circ)\), for \(0 \le m \le 12\), where \(m\) is the number of months after the middle of January.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the lowest and the highest average monthly temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the value of \(m\) at which the temperature is highest.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the two values of \(m\) at which the average temperature is 18.5 °C.

idea: The cosine part moves between \(-1\) and \(+1\). Here it is multiplied by \(-9\), so the model starts at its lowest value when \(m = 0\) and reaches its highest value half a period later.

solution.label: a
steps: \(-9\cos(30m^\circ)\) moves between \(-9\) and \(+9\), so \(T\) moves between \(14 - 9\) and \(14 + 9\).

solution.label: b
steps: The period is \(\dfrac{360}{30} = 12\) months. The lowest value is at \(m = 0\), so the highest is half a period later.

solution.label: c
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(T(2.5) = 14 - 9\cos(75^\circ) = 11.67\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: Graph \(y = 14 - 9\cos(30x^\circ)\) for \(0 \le x \le 12\) and find where it meets \(y = 18.5\).
The two answers are the same distance, 2 months, either side of the hottest time, \(m = 6\).

stem: Leo is pedalling an exercise bike at a steady rate. The height of one pedal above the floor, \(h\) cm, after \(t\) seconds is modelled by \(h(t) = 17\cos(450t^\circ) + 28\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the greatest and the least height of the pedal above the floor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time taken for one complete turn of the pedal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of complete turns of the pedal in one minute.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the height of the pedal when \(t = 0.3\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the first two times at which the pedal is 36.5 cm above the floor.

idea: One turn of the pedal is one complete cycle of the cosine curve. The time for a cycle is the period, \(\dfrac{360}{b}\), and the number of cycles in a minute follows from that.

solution.label: a
steps: The cosine part moves between \(-17\) and \(+17\): \(28 + 17\) and \(28 - 17\).

solution.label: d
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(h(0.3) = 17\cos(135^\circ) + 28 = 15.97\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Graph \(y = 17\cos(450x^\circ) + 28\) and \(y = 36.5\), with a window such as \(0 \le x \le 1\), and find the first two intersections: \(t = 0.1333\ldots\) and \(t = 0.6666\ldots\)
The first is on the way down from the top and the second is on the way back up.

stem: The percentage of the Moon's face that is lit, as seen from Earth, \(t\) days after a new moon is modelled by \(F(t) = 50 - 50\cos(bt^\circ)\). One complete cycle, from new moon to the next new moon, takes 29.5 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(b = 12.2\), correct to three significant figures.
Use \(b = 12.2\) in the rest of this question.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the percentage of the Moon's face that is lit 5 days after a new moon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of days after a new moon at which exactly half of the Moon's face is first lit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of days, in one cycle, for which more than 90 % of the Moon's face is lit.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the two values of \(t\), in one cycle, at which exactly 75 % of the Moon's face is lit.

idea: At \(t = 0\) the cosine is 1, so \(F = 0\): a new moon. Half a cycle later the cosine is \(-1\), so \(F = 100\): a full moon. Draw the graph for one cycle and read the answers from it.

solution.label: a
steps: The period is 29.5 days, so \(\dfrac{360}{b} = 29.5\) and \(b = \dfrac{360}{29.5} = 12.203\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(F(5) = 50 - 50\cos(61^\circ) = 25.75\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(50 - 50\cos(12.2t^\circ) = 50\). This needs \(\cos(12.2t^\circ) = 0\), which first happens when \(12.2t = 90\).

solution.label: d
steps: Graph \(y = 50 - 50\cos(12.2x^\circ)\) and \(y = 90\). In one cycle they meet at \(t = 11.73\ldots\) and \(t = 17.77\ldots\)
The graph is above 90 between these: \(17.77\ldots - 11.73\ldots = 6.044\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Add the line \(y = 75\) to the graph and find the two intersections in one cycle: \(t = 9.836\ldots\) and \(t = 19.67\ldots\)
The first is while the lit part is growing and the second is while it is shrinking. They are the same distance either side of the full moon.

stem: The monthly sales of a garden centre, \(S\) thousand dollars, are modelled by \(S(t) = 2t + 15\sin(30t^\circ) + 40\), for \(0 \le t \le 24\), where \(t\) is the number of months after the centre opened.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the term \(2t\) and the term \(15\sin(30t^\circ)\) each tell you about the sales.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The graph of \(S\) has one local maximum point and one local minimum point for \(0 < t < 12\). Find the coordinates of each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the value of \(t\) at which the sales first reach 80 thousand dollars.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find \(S(18) - S(6)\), and explain why the answer could have been found without a calculator.

idea: This model is a straight line and a sine wave added together: a wave that climbs. Your calculator can graph the sum directly, and the maximum, minimum and intersection tools work on it as on any other graph.

solution.label: a
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(S(3) = 6 + 15\sin(90^\circ) + 40 = 6 + 15 + 40\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(2t\) increases by 2 for every month, whatever the season.
\(15\sin(30t^\circ)\) moves between \(-15\) and \(+15\) and repeats every \(\dfrac{360}{30} = 12\) months.
solution.answer: \(2t\): sales are growing steadily by 2 thousand dollars a month. \(15\sin(30t^\circ)\): a seasonal rise and fall of up to 15 thousand dollars, repeating every 12 months

solution.label: c
steps: Graph \(y = 2x + 15\sin(30x^\circ) + 40\) for \(0 \le x \le 12\) and use the maximum and minimum tools.
Maximum: \(t = 3.491\ldots\), \(S = 61.48\ldots\) Minimum: \(t = 8.508\ldots\), \(S = 42.51\ldots\)
The maximum comes a little later than \(t = 3\), where the sine wave alone peaks, because the line \(2t\) is still pushing the total upwards.

solution.label: d
steps: Add the line \(y = 80\) and widen the window to \(0 \le x \le 24\). The first intersection is at \(t = 13.84\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: The two times are exactly 12 months apart, which is one full period of the sine term, so the seasonal part is the same at both. Only the \(2t\) part changes, by \(2 \times 12\).
solution.answer: 24: the seasonal term is the same 12 months later, so the difference is just \(2 \times 12\)

stem: The demand for electricity in a town, \(D\) megawatts, is recorded every 3 hours for one day, starting at 06:00. Here \(t\) is the number of hours after 06:00.
Kai suggests the model \(D(t) = 300\sin(15t^\circ) + 900\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that Kai's model gives the recorded values at \(t = 0\), \(t = 6\) and \(t = 18\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of the numbers 900, 300 and 15 in Kai's model can be found from the table.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage error in the value that Kai's model gives for \(t = 3\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use Kai's model to find the first time of day after 12:00 at which the demand is 750 megawatts.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A quadratic model is fitted through the points \((0,\,900)\), \((6,\,1200)\) and \((12,\,900)\). Explain why this model would be much worse than Kai's for \(t > 12\).

idea: A good model is tested against the data: check that it gives the right values where it should, measure how far off it is elsewhere, and think about whether its shape matches what really happens.

solution.label: a
steps: Set your calculator to degrees. \(D(0) = 300\sin(0^\circ) + 900 = 900\).

solution.label: b
steps: 900 is the principal axis, halfway between the greatest and least values: \(\dfrac{1200 + 600}{2}\).
300 is the amplitude, half of the distance between them: \(\dfrac{1200 - 600}{2}\).
The pattern repeats after 24 hours, so the period is 24 and \(b = \dfrac{360}{24} = 15\).
solution.answer: 900 = middle of 1200 and 600; 300 = half of their difference; 15 = 360 ÷ 24, from the 24-hour period

solution.label: c
steps: Model: \(D(3) = 300\sin(45^\circ) + 900 = 1112.1\ldots\) The recorded value, 1105, is the exact value.
\[\varepsilon = \left|\frac{1112.1\ldots - 1105}{1105}\right| \times 100 = 0.645\ldots\]

solution.label: d
steps: 12:00 is \(t = 6\). Graph the model and \(y = 750\), and find the first intersection after \(t = 6\): \(t = 14\).
Check: \(300\sin(210^\circ) + 900 = 300 \times (-0.5) + 900 = 750\). Fourteen hours after 06:00 is 20:00.

solution.label: e
steps: A parabola through those three points has its highest point at \(t = 6\) and keeps falling for ever after it. The real demand stops falling at \(t = 18\) and rises again, which a sine curve does and a parabola cannot.
solution.answer: The parabola keeps decreasing after \(t = 12\), but the real demand turns and rises again after \(t = 18\)
